```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

Here, we are going to cover decision trees (or "trees") and random forests.  A tree works by creating splits within the predictor space such that outcome values within each sub-region are progressively more similar. Visually, these splits form a tree‑like structure: each split creates a new branch, and the final branches—where no further splitting is useful—are called leaves. The leaves will bear a value that is:

-   the **most common** outcome in that branch (for a categorical or binary outcomes), or
-   the **average** outcome in that branch (for continuous outcomes)

Predictions for new observations are made on the basis of this tree. 

A single tree tends to overfit the data it's fed, resulting in incorrect predictions when tested on new data. In random forests, many trees are created from the same data and the average of their predictions is assigned to a new observation. This can be a powerful way to increase prediction accuracy. 

We will look at an application to Bank Telemarketing Data (available [here](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/222/bank+marketing)), which is a popular dataset for testing ML algorithms. It's a real-world data set of a phone-based marketing campaign by a Portuguese banking institution. The aim of the campaign was to get clients to subscribe to a term deposit. 

The data set contains four Comma Separated Values files (".csv"). We will be using 'banks.csv', which has 10% of the observations in the original data and fewer input variables. Using this smaller file makes it easier to run machine‑learning methods that require more computing power.

Note: For this walkthrough, we are assuming that you are already familiar with cross-validation - a technique commonly used to choose model hyperparameters. A cross-validation walkthrough is available in ECLR on this [link](https://datasquad.github.io/ECLR/R_CrossValidation/R_CrossValidation.html).

# Setup and Data Upload

Let's load some necessary packages.

```{r cars, warning= FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(readxl)                                                     # to read the data
library(tidyverse)                                                    
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)                                                   # the last three packages help with data transformation
library(tree)                                                       # for building trees
library(randomForest)                                               # for random forests
```

Let’s load the bank telemarketing data.

```{r}
bank <- read.table("C:/Users/shonk/OneDrive/Imports/sukanya.honkote@manchester.ac.uk - Dropbox/TA/2024-25/Introduction to Causal Inference using Machine Learning/Random Forests/bank.csv", 
  header = TRUE,
  sep = ";", 
  na.strings = c("", " ")) 

str(bank)
```

The data consists of 17 variables and 4521 observations. The outcome of interest is the one simply called <code style="color: #8a2be2;">y</code>. <code style="color: #8a2be2;">y = no</code> indicates the client did not subscribe to the term deposit.

The variable descriptions are pasted from bank-names.txt, which is provided along with the data:

   1) age (numeric)
   2) job : type of job (categorical: "admin.","unknown","unemployed","management","housemaid","entrepreneur","student",
                                       "blue-collar","self-employed","retired","technician","services") 
   3) marital : marital status (categorical: "married","divorced","single"; note: "divorced" means divorced or widowed)
   4) education (categorical: "unknown","secondary","primary","tertiary")
   5) default: has credit in default? (binary: "yes","no")
   6) balance: average yearly balance, in euros (numeric) 
   7) housing: has housing loan? (binary: "yes","no")
   8) loan: has personal loan? (binary: "yes","no")
   # related with the last contact of the current campaign:
   9) contact: contact communication type (categorical: "unknown","telephone","cellular") 
  10) day: last contact day of the month (numeric)
  11) month: last contact month of year (categorical: "jan", "feb", "mar", ..., "nov", "dec")
  12) duration: last contact duration, in seconds (numeric)
   # other attributes:
  13) campaign: number of contacts performed during this campaign and for this client (numeric, includes last contact)
  14) pdays: number of days that passed by after the client was last contacted from a previous campaign (numeric, -1 means client was not previously contacted)
  15) previous: number of contacts performed before this campaign and for this client (numeric)
  16) poutcome: outcome of the previous marketing campaign (categorical: "unknown","other","failure","success")
  17) y: has the client subscribed a term deposit? (binary: "yes","no")

Notice, all the factor variables have been loaded as character variables. In order to proceed with the exercise, we will need to convert them to factor variables.

```{r}
bank %<>% mutate(across(where(is.character),as_factor))               # converts characters into factor variables in one go
str(bank)                                                             # check if characters have been converted into factors
```

Have a look at summary statistics to understand the data better. 

```{r}
summary(bank)
```

<div style="background-color: #e6f5ff; border-left: 6px solid #0066cc; padding: 10px; margin-num: 10px;">
Q: Are there any missing values in the data? Options: Y/N. Answer: N. If there were any true missing values in the data, their count within each variable would appear at the bottom of their summary statistics. Notice, however, that <code style="color: #8a2be2;">unknown</code> is a commonly occurring value for some of the factor variables. These values were coded as <code style="color: #8a2be2;">unknown</code> rather than <code style="color: #8a2be2;">NA</code>, perhaps because many statistical programming commands would fail if the data contained true missing values.
</div>

Let's look at the outcome variable more closely. 

```{r}
prop.table(table(bank$y)) * 100
```

Only a tenth of clients subscribed to term deposits during the telemarketing campaign. Such imbalance is quite common in real-world data. However, this results in machine-learning models becoming very good at predicting the majority class (<code style="color: #8a2be2;">y = no</code>), while struggling to learn patterns related to the minority class (<code style="color: #8a2be2;">y = yes</code>). There are specialised techniques for addressing this issue, but to keep the exercise straightforward, we will not apply them here.

# Handling 'unknown' values

It is worth considering if something can be done about unknown values in the data. If they are left as is, and a tree split is performed along this value, it can decrease  interpretability of the tree. 

Consider the variable <code style="color: #8a2be2;">poutcome</code>, which has a large share of unknown. From the variable descriptions <code style="color: #8a2be2;">pdays = -1</code> means the client was not previously contacted. The following check shows that all the unknown cases in <code style="color: #8a2be2;">poutcome</code> were the ones previously not contacted.

```{r}
summary(bank$poutcome[bank$pdays == -1])                            # tells us the value of poutcome if pdays = -1 
summary(bank$pdays[bank$poutcome == "unknown"])                     # tells us the value of pdays if poutcome = unknown 
```

We can replace <code style="color: #8a2be2;">poutcome = unknown</code> with a more representative value. Let's call this new value <code style="color: #8a2be2;">No previous contact</code> and recode the variable.

```{r}
levels(bank$poutcome)[match("unknown",levels(bank$poutcome))] <- "no previous contact"
summary(bank$poutcome)
```

<div style="background-color: #e6f2ff; border-left: 6px solid #0066cc; padding: 10px; margin-num: 10px;">
Question: Notice summary stats of <code style="color: #8a2be2;">education</code> and <code style="color: #8a2be2;">contact</code>. They also have a considerable share of unknowns. What do you think is the best solution to this? a. Replace unknowns with the mode of each variable. b. Check if the unknowns are correlated with any other client characteristics available in the data c. Leave it as it is for now, and come back to it later. d. Drop <code style="color: #8a2be2;">contact</code> from the dataset as it has a large share of unknown, and keep <code style="color: #8a2be2;">education</code> as is. e. Other. Answer: (This could be a poll question, as there is no right answer.) We can consider each option, one-by-one. (a) is simple to execute and may work if unknowns are not correlated with other characteristics. (b) can provide a more informed manner of going about replacing unknown values, (c) is the simplest to start with. However, if the variables with lots of unknown values are important in prediction, then dealing with it becomes important for interpretability. (d) may *not* be a good move to start with, in case, the variables are useful in prediction. (e) is an interesting choice. Why did you choose that? In this exercise, we are going to choose (c).
</div>

# Estimating the tree

To fit a tree to the data and evaluate it for its accuracy in prediction, we place the observations randomly into training and test sets. The training set will be used to fit a classification tree that models <code style="color: #8a2be2;">y</code>. All other variables will be provided as inputs.

```{r}
set.seed(6)                                                            # initialises the random sampling 
train_id <- sample(1:nrow(bank),nrow(bank)/2)                                 
train <- bank[train_id, ]
test <- bank[-train_id, ]
tree.bank <- tree(y ~ ., train)                                        # fits a tree to the training data
```

A plot of the fitted tree produces the following:

```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=12}
plot(tree.bank)                                                   
text(tree.bank, pretty = 0) 
```

We can see which variables have been split and at what value.The splits are *internal nodes*, which can result in a branch or leaf. *Each internal node is labelled based on the condition governing the left-hand of the split.* For e.g. at the top-most split, the left-hand branch contains all the observations where <code style="color: #8a2be2;">duration < 219.5</code> (approx. 3.5  minutes). The right-hand branch contains all the observations where <code style="color: #8a2be2;">duration >= 219.5</code>. The region where the predictor space is not split any further is a leaf or a *terminal node*. The leaf carries the value of the outcome predicted for that region. In a classification problem, each leaf is assigned the majority class within that leaf. 

<div style="background-color: #e6f2ff; border-left: 6px solid #0066cc; padding: 10px; margin-num: 10px;">
Q:Test your understanding. If call-duration was between 4-10 minutes and <code style="color: #8a2be2;">poutcome = success</code>, what was the most likely outcome if a call was placed in July? [Options: <code style="color: #8a2be2;">y = yes</code> <code style="color: #8a2be2;">y = no</code> Answer: <code style="color: #8a2be2;">y = yes</code>. Note: 'tree solution.jpeg' should be attached as solution.]
</div>

Some of the splits yield branches having the same predicted outcome. For example, the first two terminal nodes from the left of the plot (internal node of <code style="color: #8a2be2;">pdays < 68.5</code>) have the same classification of <code style="color: #8a2be2;">no</code>. Why does the tree algorithm perform the split in that case? The algorithm may still perform the split to increase *node purity* i.e. the share of observations belonging to a single class in the branch/leaf increases.

You may wonder why the algorithm did not consider producing more final nodes. The algorithm stops producing more nodes when either the nodes become too small or if the improvement of the data fit becomes too small. These stopping criteria are controlled by the options in the <code style="color: #8a2be2;">tree.control</code> function. The <code style="color: #8a2be2;">mincut</code> (default setting = 5) and <code style="color: #8a2be2;">minsize</code> (=10) options control the minimum node size and <code style="color: #8a2be2;">mindev</code> (=0.01) the required improvement.

<div style="background-color: #e6f2ff; border-left: 6px solid #0066cc; padding: 10px; margin-num: 10px;">
Information tab from Ralf's text: How did the tree function decide to split? "This is not the place where we will spend time on explaining the.....OLS type problems."]
</div>

The <code style="color: #8a2be2;">summary ()</code> function will give some useful tree statistics.

```{r}
summary(tree.bank) 
```

Only 7 of the 16 available predictors are used in tree construction. The size of the tree, which is a measure of tree complexity is 13 (number of terminal nodes). The residual mean deviance measures how well the tree fits the data. It is the deviance divided by the degrees of freedom i.e. number of observations minus the tree-size. Misclassification error is similar to deviance, measuring the proportion of observations that are incorrectly classified—i.e., those whose actual outcome differs from the majority class of the leaf they belong to. In this case, it’s 9.69 percent. 

<div style="background-color: #e6f2ff; border-left: 6px solid #0066cc; padding: 10px; margin-num: 10px;">
Test your understanding. Which of these measures penalises tree complexity? Options a. Tree-size b. Residual mean deviance c. Misclassification error. Answer: (b). A more complex tree with have a higher tree size. Residual mean deviance penalises large tree sizes by dividing deviance by the degrees of freedom.
</div>

It can be instructive to see the subscription probabilities for the branches/leaves. These are saved in <code style="color: #8a2be2;">tree.bank$frame</code>.

```{r}
tree.bank$frame$yprob
```

The random forest algorithm aims to maximise node purity, and so the the classification probabilities will tend to 0 or 1. Note, there are 13 terminal nodes and 12 internal nodes giving rise to 25 outcome probabilities.

There are other pieces of information about the estimated tree you can get from the frame object in your estimated tree. For instance <code style="color: #8a2be2;">n</code> gives the number of observations at each node. 

```{r}
tree.bank$frame$n 
```

To understand which nodes these are referring too, see how they are numbered. 

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("Tree bank nodes.png")
```

For instance, node 1 represents the entire predictor space before the first split occurs, therefore it contains 2260 observations. The numbering can be verified by typing <code style="color: #8a2be2;">tree.bank$frame</code>. 

# Evaluation

We evaluate the performance of the fitted tree on the test data using the <code style="color: #8a2be2;">predict()</code> function. To ensure that the predictions are in terms of classes, we need to provide <code style="color: #8a2be2;">type = “class”</code> as an argument.

```{r}

b.tree.pred <- predict(tree.bank, test, type = "class")           # predicting outcomes in test data set
test.y <- test$y                                                  # list with actual outcomes in test data
table(b.tree.pred , test.y)                                       # Confusion matrix
```

The table displays how accurately the tree predicted the values of subscription for the test set observations. Model **accuracy** is (1860+140)/2261 = 0.8846 i.e. the share of observations that are predicted correctly. The **sensitivity** of the model, given by the share of positive outcomes that are correctly predicted: 140/257 = 0.54. This is an improvement on the unconditional probability of subscribing (11.68%).

# Tree Pruning

So far there was no penalty for tree complexity. This step should be considered as the tree algorithm will likely overfit the data, which can lead to poor performance on the test set. We set a penalty $\alpha > 0$ for tree size. For any $\alpha$, the goal is to find the optimal subtree (from the original large tree) that minimizes the combined measure:

$$ 
\text{Total error of the Subtree} + \alpha (\text{Size of the Subtree})
$$ The larger the $\alpha$ the simpler the tree.

To find the appropriate $\alpha$, we use cross-validation. The <code style="color: #8a2be2;">cv.tree()</code> function progressively increases $\alpha$ value and obtains trees of different sizes from the original tree. These subtrees are then validated in the hold-out fold of the data. The error of the subtrees are averaged across all the folds and stored by the algorithm.

```{r}
set.seed(17)                                                       
cv.bank <- cv.tree(tree.bank, FUN = prune.misclass)                                      
cv.bank                                                 
```

The summary output shows the size of each subtree drawn from <code style="color: #8a2be2;">tree.bank</code> for a given <code style="color: #8a2be2;">k</code> (the penalty that we denoted by $\alpha$). <code style="color: #8a2be2;">dev</code> is the number of cross-validation errors, associated with that subtree.

We plot the error rate as a function of the penalty and tree size.

```{r}
# Plotting the error rate as a function of size and k
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
plot(cv.bank$size, cv.bank$dev, type = "b") 
plot(cv.bank$k, cv.bank$dev, type = "b")
```

The tree size giving the lowest error is one with 4 or 7 nodes. The corresponding penalties are 5 and 2, respectively.

Let's visualise the pruned tree. We first prune the large tree by providing the optimal tree-size and then ask R to plot it. 

```{r}
tree.b.prune <- prune.tree(tree.bank, best = 4, method = "misclass")  
plot(tree.b.prune)
text(tree.b.prune, pretty = 0)
```

Notice how the branches have fallen off the original tree? And, only <code style="color: #8a2be2;">duration</code> and <code style="color: #8a2be2;">poutcome</code> remain.

Let's check if pruning helps in achieving better prediction accuracy. We use the same steps we used when evaluating the performance of the unpruned tree (<code style="color: #8a2be2;">tree.bank</code>) to find out.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
b.tree.prune.pred <- predict(XXXX, test, type = "class")       # fill in the correct input     
table(Predicted = b.tree.prune.pred , Actual = test.y)                  
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
b.tree.prune.pred <- predict(tree.b.prune, test, type = "class")
table(Predicted = b.tree.prune.pred , Actual = test.y)                  
```

Model accuracy increases by a small fraction (approx. 0.0035), while the sensitivity declines. Ideally, we would want a method that increases both.

<div style="background-color: #e6f2ff; border-left: 6px solid #0066cc; padding: 10px; margin-num: 10px;">
Ralf's information tab: Does pruning always deliver the same result?
</div>

# Random Forests

Trees suffer from high variance. You would get a different tree with each random subset of the data. You can see this by fitting a tree to the test data:

```{r}
tree.bt.test <- tree(y ~ ., test)
summary(tree.bt.test)
```

Compared to <code style="color: #8a2be2;">tree.bank</code>, the tree size is smaller and fewer variables are used in tree construction. This is a symptom of high variance in the model. When  variance of a model is high, predictions based on it will be less accurate. A large enough data set will not get rid of the problem of high variance of a tree. Tree pruning will also not necessarily improve accuracy.

Random forests is one solution to the issue of high-variance of trees. It involves building multiple decision trees using bootstrapped training samples. Bootstrapping implies taking repeated random samples from a single training data set. In addition, splits are carried out only by considering a random subset of predictors. Typically, the number of predictors chosen is the square root of predictors ($\sqrt{p}$). This allows the algorithm to build trees that are different from each other, giving weaker predictors more of a chance to appear in the splits. When the predictions of these trees are averaged, the variance is lower leading to better accuracy in predictions.

We will use the <code style="color: #8a2be2;">randomForest</code> package in R to apply random forests to the data. Setting <code style="color: #8a2be2;">importance = TRUE</code> prompts the function to calculate importance measures for each predictor.

```{r}
set.seed(131)                                            
rf.bt <- randomForest(y ~ ., data = train, importance = TRUE)              
print(rf.bt)
```

The summary of the output tells us that the model is trained by creating 500 trees using 4 randomly selected predictors for each split. 500 is the default number of trees, although it can be changed using the option <code style="color: #8a2be2;">ntrees</code>. The Out Of Bag (OOB) error is the average error in prediction of training observations not included in the bootstrapped samples. Averaging the predictions of 500 trees is generally considered adequate for stabilising the OOB error rate.

While we cannot create a tree-like plot after applying random forests, we can still generate variable importance scores for all of the predictors. The function <code style="color: #8a2be2;">varImpPlot()</code> generate plots where variables are displayed in decreasing order of importance. This provides a clear picture of which variables are useful in classification.


```{r}
varImpPlot(rf.bt)                                         
```

Two kinds of scores are being generated: (i) Mean Decrease in Accuracy i.e. the decrease in OOB accuracy when the variable is excluded, and (ii) Mean Decrease in Gini i.e. the total decrease in Gini Index from splitting on the variable.(Gini Index is explained in 'How did the tree function decide to split?' tab in Estimating the Tree section)

There are slight differences in ranking of variables across the plots, but they are generally in agreement with one another, and with the tree we fit earlier, in that <code style="color: #8a2be2;">duration</code> is the variable of primary importance. 

The actual scores can be obtained by typing the following:

```{r}
importance(rf.bt)                                          # displays variable importance scores
```

The last two columns are displaying the importance scores with higher numbers meaning that variables are more important. Note, there could be negative scores.

Now we should test how well the model works on test data. The <code style="color: #8a2be2;">predict()</code> function will cycle the new data points through all the 500 trees of the forest and predict the class of the point using a majority vote. 


```{r, eval = FALSE}
rf.pred <- predict(XXX, test, type = "class")                   # fill the missing inputs  
table(Predicted = ZZZ, Actual = YYY)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
rf.pred <- predict(rf.bt, test, type = "class")                   
table(Predicted = rf.pred, Actual = test.y)
```

The test accuracy increases more significantly this time (approx. 1%), however sensitivity decreases even further. This can happen while applying random forests if the outcome is very imbalanced and the model depends on only a few of the predictors.

# Further extensions

To further improve the effectiveness of the random forests method, let's consider results based on - (1) dropping less important predictors, and (2) bootstrapping on all the predictors (called 'bagging').

Using the variable importance plots, we drop the least important variables. Here, the four least important variables - education, campaign, loan and default are dropped as an example. This way more relevant variables are being used in tree construction.

```{r}
set.seed(131)                                            
rf.bt2 <- randomForest(y ~ . - loan - default - campaign - education, data = train, importance = TRUE)  
rf.pred2 <- predict(rf.bt2, test, type = "class")                   
table(rf.pred2, test.y)  
```

Based on the confusion matrix, we get only a slight improvement in accuracy and sensitivity, compared to <code style="color: #8a2be2;">rf.pred</code>.

For bagging, all we need to do is instruct <code style="color: #8a2be2;">randomForests()</code> to use all the predictors instead of a subset. The <code style="color: #8a2be2;">mtry</code> option allows us to specify the number of predictors to be used in fitting all the trees. We set it equal to the maximum number of predictors.


```{r}
set.seed(131)                                            
bag.bt <- randomForest(y ~ ., data = train, mtry = 16)              
bag.pred <- predict(bag.bt, test, type = "class")         
table(bag.pred, test.y)
```

We see that random forests performs better in terms of accuracy, however bagging is better at predicting positive values. By considering only a subset of predictors, random forests may be missing the predictors that matter for prediction of positive values. With bagging, that's not an issue as it always considers all the predictors.

# Summary of results and conclusion

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning= FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Unpruned Tree", "Pruning", "Random Forest", "Random Forest with Feature Elimination", "Bagging"),
  Accuracy = c(0.885,0.888,0.895,0.896,0.893)*100,
  Sensitivity = c(0.545,0.471,0.354,0.366,0.408 )*100
)

kable(results, caption = "<div style='text-align:center; color:black;'><b>Model Accuracy and Sensitivity (%)</b></div>") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "14em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "6em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "6em")
```

In this walkthrough, we used a variety of tree-based methods for a classification problem using a real-world dataset. Trees and forests can also be used for handling regression problems (which involve continuous outcomes) - to see a practical example of R-code, see Section 8.3.2 of Introduction to Statistical Learning, referenced below.

While a lot of work goes into improving accuracy of tree-based methods, they remain a powerful and widely used tool for prediction.
